name: Gyropup

battery.model: DCB609 FLEXVOLT 9.0 Ah x 2, 20 V mode, in series (D65)
battery.price_note: 2 x $259 (The Power Tool Store (thepowertoolstore.com), Shopify store JSON read 2026-10-25; other sellers $386-$398)

specs.basis: D65: each pack in 20 V mode is 5S3P, 9.0 Ah, 180 Wh rated; two in series make a 10S3P bus, 36 V nominal, about 41 V full, 30 V empty (3.0 V a cell, enforced by the robot)

hardware_allowance.note: bearings, shoulder bolts, inserts, fasteners, wiring

notes: Default: two DeWalt DCB609 FLEXVOLT 9.0 Ah packs, each in 20 V mode, in series in two 20 V dock adapters: a 10S bus, 36 V nominal, 30-41 V (D65; the 'battery' part is the pair, battery_count 1). The RS-04s (24-60 V) keep 19 V of regen headroom, so there is no regen clamp. The wheels run from two Flipsky 75100 VESCs (14-84 V). A TRACO TEP 150-4812WI (18-75 V in, 12 V) feeds the J501 and the 12 V rail (the DDR-120C-24 starts at 33.6 V, above the empty pack). Tool packs leave under-voltage and current limits to the tool, so the robot enforces 3.0 V/cell (30 V) and a current limit. An 80 A MRBF fuse at the battery and an anti-spark switch (D55); a microcontroller with CAN runs the 1 kHz balance loop. No e-stop button or contactor on the robot: the radio stop (D34, D55).

requirements: steady 1 kHz loop independent of Linux
CAN to the motors (it owns the motor bus)
CAN to the J501's built-in CAN-FD for the Jetson link (a second bus, or one shared CAN-FD bus)
UART (TTL or RS-232) for the VN-100
options: a microcontroller with CAN from the user's own boards (to be named)
balance_controller.status: assumed: WeAct STM32G474 core with two CAN transceivers (D7), until the user names a board

head_payload.note: Budget for the head payload interface (docs/head-payload.md); the turret itself is developed separately.
